stories.body:
Invasive alien brambles have been spreading across South Africa since the early 1900s, having come from North America and Europe. All brambles fall within the genus Rubus . Their common names in South Africa are braam (Afrikaans), ijingijolo (isiZulu) and monoko-metsi (seSotho).

Over the decades, these plants have crept into tree plantations, pastures and native grasslands. Dense, thorny thickets now choke open spaces, and impede livestock and wildlife movement. They restrict access to water, smother young trees used for timber, interfere with plantation management and disrupt roadsides.

They have become one of the most widespread and damaging weeds, though it’s hard to estimate how much land they cover because satellite imagery doesn’t capture them in grasslands and they “hide” under forest canopy.

Beyond ruining hiking experiences and doing agricultural damage, these infestations also displace native vegetation and negatively affect specialist flower-visitors like butterflies .

People have tried to manage invasive brambles, yet traditional chemical and mechanical controls don’t work. This is due to the sheer scale of the invasions, costs that are too high for low-value land, rugged terrain that limits access, and the plant’s ability to resprout from rootstocks or re-emerge from bird-dispersed seeds.

Consequently, there is an urgent need for additional management tools. Biological control (biocontrol) has been considered in South Africa, but never tried.

My research focuses on biological control of weeds, which works by introducing specialised natural enemies from the plant’s native range (where they came from originally) to suppress its growth or reproduction. Before any natural enemy is released, it undergoes rigorous testing in quarantine to make sure it only damages the weed. By using tested, host-specific natural enemies that cannot survive on any other host, biocontrol aims to restore ecosystems with minimal disturbance. Biocontrol offers a proven safety record that far outweighs the hazards of traditional control methods.

The first step is to be sure what the weed is, where it came from, what its natural enemies are and how much of a problem it is.

Recently our research team published the results of a study into brambles in South Africa to start answering these questions. Until recently, the most damaging brambles in this country were treated as a single species, Rubus cuneifolius Pursh . Research has since separated the dominant invasive species into three taxa. Our study concludes that biological control of Rubus sect. Cuneifolii and two forms of R. sect. Arguti is feasible and may be a suitable option to manage the impact of the weed in South Africa.

Identifying the enemy

Establishing a clear identity for the target plant is essential to finding natural enemies. This requirement has been a major stumbling block to bramble biocontrol.

In the past, invasion biologists and botanists lacked clarity on which species the brambles in South Africa belonged to, and which ones were driving invasions. This was complicated by the tendency of brambles to hybridise, both across invasive species and between invasive and native species. (South Africa has several native brambles that need to be protected.)

Read more: Why plants need an identity

Overcoming the identification hurdle and others became the aim of research carried out at the Agricultural Research Council and at the Centre for Biological Control , attached to Rhodes University, from 2018 on.

At the same time, a world-leading Czech batologist (a person who studies brambles), Michal Sochor, was conducting studies to untangle South Africa’s bramble diversity, in collaboration with John Manning of the South African National Biodiversity Institute. This work revealed a complex mix of 18 pure taxa and 12 hybrid lines of Rubus in South Africa.

It separated the dominant invasive species, previously identified as Rubus cuneifolius , into three taxa (an upright form and two sprawling forms).

We then evaluated 91 highly affected forestry, grassland and roadside sites to map Rubus spp. distributions, genetic structures and morphological (shape) traits.

These revealed that the upright form ( Rubus sect. Cuneifolii ) was the most widespread invader in the grassland biome, dominating 42 of the 69 accessible sites. In KwaZulu-Natal province, it heavily invades open grasslands and timber plantations as a single, genetically uniform clone. No hybridisation was recorded.

The sprawling forms ( R. sect. Arguti ) were recorded at 26 sites, mainly along roadsides and in disturbed habitats across three provinces (KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga and Limpopo). These plants were genetically divided into five distinct genotypes showing clear geographic clustering.

Cost-benefit analysis

Anyone spending time outdoors in South Africa is likely familiar with wild brambles, having enjoyed picking and eating their fruit, often without knowing which species they were. Foraging from wild populations even supports small cottage industries, such as making jam and preserves, brewing small batches of gin, and selling whole berries in local farm-stalls.

To ensure future management strategies avoid potential conflicts of interest, our research included a socio-economic study of the economic value of these Rubus species.

This confirmed that alien brambles generate positive private value through wild berry harvesting, dietary supplementation and small-scale processing. But our research found that environmental and management costs outweigh these local benefits. The cost to government of clearing the weeds was 13.5 times greater than the recorded financial benefits (which were all in one province, the Free State).

Wild harvesting proved to be a “nice to have” rather than a vital part of local livelihoods or daily nutrition.

Decisive control measures are therefore needed.

Next, find enemies

Biocontrol should provide a helpful tool in the management of invasive Rubus in South Africa, as it has in several other countries.

Thanks to a much clearer understanding of where Rubus fits into the plant world, what seemed like an intractable challenge in the 1980s and 1990s is becoming a manageable research project. This is because we can now determine the plants’ exact origin to ensure that the right or most closely associated natural enemies are collected and considered for further testing.

The next steps are to track down populations of Rubus in the US which closely match those in South Africa, survey them for natural enemies (preferably an insect that damages the stem or leaf), and select one or more of these for host-specificity trials.

It is entirely realistic that an effective biocontrol agent could be released within the next decade for South Africa’s invasive North American brambles, hopefully reducing their vigour and competitiveness while paving the way for cost-effective integrated management.

stories.body:
Toxic Pressure

Co-published with The Frontier

Reporting Highlights

Citation’s Track Record: Citation Oil & Gas is named more than any other company in an Oklahoma database of pollution reports and other rule violations — over 1,000 times in the past decade.

Pollution Without Punishment: Regulatory agency staff repeatedly recommended the state punish Citation. Instead, agency bosses allowed the company to restart operations without consequence.

Regulators Rarely Regulate: Our analysis found that less than a third of enforcement cases filed by Oklahoma’s oil division since 2023 have resulted in punishment.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

In June 2023, staff at an Oklahoma regulatory agency were fed up. The state isn’t known for cracking down on oil and gas companies for polluting the environment, but for over a year, the staff had been building a case to punish Citation Oil & Gas, one of the nation’s largest privately owned oil companies.

About 30 miles north of the Texas border, toxic wastewater was gushing from the ground outside the small city of Ardmore. In the mile-wide oil field known as the Bayou, an oily sheen glistened on creeks and long streaks of salt scarred the land. The so-called purges, bubbling up among stands of oak and walnut trees, also threatened drinking water sources, drawing attention from the Environmental Protection Agency, according to a federal report.

State investigators pinned the blame on Citation’s injection wells, which pump wastewater from oil production back underground at high pressures and volumes in order to produce more oil. But this injection came with risks.

Days earlier, the agency had asked Citation to cut injection pressures in half. The company refused, prompting staff at the oil division of the Oklahoma Corporation Commission, the state’s oil and gas regulator, to recommend an official punishment through the agency’s court system.

“This will be an important case to get some of these purges stopped and particularly concerning Citation’s operations,” Danny Ray, an agency manager at the time, emailed his colleagues.

He restated the urgency three days later in an email to oil division leaders and Citation officials: “We consider this an emergency situation that needs to be addressed promptly.”

To stop the flow of wastewater, the agency temporarily shut down the Bayou’s 22 injection wells — all but three of which were owned by Citation — kicking off a yearlong fight over the terms under which injection could restart.

Under state rules, companies must not pollute, and oil and gas regulators at the Corporation Commission can revoke injection permits and issue fines to those that violate regulations.

But agency leadership ultimately did not follow staff guidance to punish Citation through the commission’s administrative law court. Instead, in April 2024, state officials, including the oil division’s then-Director Robyn Strickland, would allow Citation to restart injection at higher-than-recommended pressures.

Agency leaders’ reluctance to punish Citation reflects a longstanding pattern of Oklahoma regulators letting oil companies contaminate drinking water , farmland and people’s homes with scant consequences, The Frontier and ProPublica have found in a yearlong investigation .

In fact the commission has no record of ever fining or completing an enforcement case against Citation, the company named more than any other in the agency’s database of pollution reports and other rule violations, listed more than 1,000 times over the past decade. That’s hundreds more incidents than any other operator, including comparably sized companies. In recent years, purges linked to Citation include some of Oklahoma’s longest, most damaging oil field pollution events.

Current and former employees at the Oklahoma Corporation Commission describe top agency officials as wary of going after habitual violators like Citation. Citation has become Oklahoma’s second-largest well owner after taking over collections of aging, low-producing wells from oil giants that have largely left the state for more lucrative oil fields in Texas and elsewhere; the company acquired its Bayou wells in 2010. Regulators treat Citation gently, current and former agency employees say, because the company holds onto aging wells that are worth little — wells that could easily become a financial liability for the state if Citation were to sell or walk away from them.

A spokesperson for the Oklahoma Corporation Commission declined to answer questions about the regulatory agency’s handling of Citation’s record, noting the possibility of future enforcement actions or litigation involving the company.

“The OCC Oil and Gas Conservation Division must remain mindful of its regulatory and adjudicatory responsibilities and avoid making public statements that could potentially affect future proceedings or legal considerations,” spokesperson Jack Damrill said in an email.

Strickland has since left the agency for a job as chief projects officer for the Interstate Oil and Gas Compact Commission , a quasi-governmental organization that often advocates for industry interests. She did not respond to requests for comment.

A Citation executive declined to comment in response to written questions.

Regulators in other jurisdictions have at times come down hard on Citation, which owns wells in 11 other states. In 2017, the company settled with the U.S. Department of Justice for $2.25 million over allegations of underpaid royalties from drilling on federal land in Wyoming, though the settlement did not rule that the company was liable in the case. And in 2025, Utah reached a $700,000 settlement with the company after a crude oil and wastewater spill. Texas and Colorado have also fined Citation in recent years for violations.

“Citation has been the thorn in my side for a long time,” said a current manager at the Oklahoma agency who spoke on the condition of anonymity to protect their job. “They just operate however they want. They’ve had major pollution issues, and you can’t really touch them.”

Preparing a Case for Punishment

In November 2023, five months into the wells’ shutdown, Citation was getting antsy. Its officials had repeatedly demanded permission to restart their wells and had even challenged the state through the commission’s court to prove the connection between the Bayou purges and its operations. Regulators and company officials packed into a small conference room in the Oklahoma Corporation Commission’s Oklahoma City headquarters to discuss how that might happen. More than a dozen others joined via video.

On the state’s side, a team of consultants took the lead, displaying a report with evidence that tied Citation’s injection to the wastewater that gushed to the surface in the Bayou. The state had hired the environmental engineering firm Halff earlier that year on a $550,000 contract to investigate the fast-growing number of oil field wastewater eruptions around Oklahoma. The consultants and agency staff presented a unified front in identifying the problem: Citation’s nearly two dozen Bayou injection wells were operating at unsafely high pressures, according to a video recording of the meeting obtained by The Frontier and ProPublica. Over the years, the injected wastewater had shattered underground rock layers, allowing the toxic fluid to spread uncontrollably.

“You definitely have overpressurization,” Carolyn May, Halff’s director of environmental remediation, told Citation officials as she presented her team’s calculations, which were based on well records, field data collected by agency staff and a standard set by the federal government. “It’s allowing that rock to fracture.”

The consultants were meant to serve as independent experts to mediate any disagreements within the agency over what to do about the wastewater eruptions, according to current and former commission officials.

In the meeting, May and agency staffers ticked off a number of problems with Citation’s wells that regulators had overlooked for years. Not only had they allowed the company to inject wastewater at excessive pressures, regulators had also given out more than a dozen exemptions to testing and well-construction standards that endangered groundwater. Several wells had checkered compliance records; agency documents noted that one had been in “perpetual violation” of its permit for “nine years running,” injecting tens of millions of gallons of wastewater beyond the legal limit.

Citation’s active wells weren’t the only issue, they said. Nearby were dozens of abandoned, unplugged wells that offered the pressurized wastewater open pathways to reach shallow freshwater sources and the surface. May singled out a handful of those wells that especially troubled her team, and oil division deputy director Mike McGinnis suggested that Citation permanently plug them.

May noted that imaging below the surface by agency staff showed a distinct plume of highly polluted wastewater rising from deep underground, where injection took place. This posed a threat to the freshwater sources beneath the Bayou, she said — water that some residents rely on for drinking and cooking. “That’s our primary concern here.”

The consultants were not alone in this fear. Earlier in 2023, the Environmental Protection Agency had warned of “potential endangerment to underground sources of drinking water” in the Bayou from oil field injection. Groundwater tests taken near the purge sites showed evidence of oil field wastewater pollution, including high levels of salt, bromide and the carcinogen benzene, which exceeded the EPA drinking water standard by five times.

For its part, Citation came to the meeting armed with a very different argument: the pollution was caused by a combination of historic oil drilling and recent rainfall — not by the company.

It was a claim the company had repeatedly made, especially in the months since the agency had shut down its wells. To bolster its case, the company’s consultants had produced a series of detailed reports citing the area’s history of oil production, along with Citation’s own water testing data. Oil drilling began in the Bayou in the 1920s, a time of lawless extraction, and for decades, companies would simply dump their wastewater into large, unlined pits, allowing the fluid to seep into the ground. Old pollution that saturated the land was being flushed to the surface by rainfall, the reports argued. Each one concluded that there was no link between Citation’s injection and the Bayou pollution.

At the meeting with regulators, company representatives reiterated these arguments. Jeff Lewis, a Citation engineering manager, assured the agency that the company’s data indicated that its wells were not behind the Bayou purges and that it could safely inject at pressures higher than Halff had recommended. He proposed that the company restart injection on its deeper wells because they were separated by layers of rock from the abandoned wells that Halff identified as likely pathways for the wastewater to surface.

Agency staff did not buy this. In prior internal meetings and emails, staff and consultants had criticized Citation’s water sampling practices as biased in favor of the company’s conclusion that rainfall was causing old pollution to resurface. There was no question that old pollution covered the Bayou, but in recent purges, wastewater had pushed to the surface in significant volumes, covering creek beds in layers of snow-white salt. Old pollution would not be this forceful, according to internal documents written by agency staff.

“A purge is created by pressure and is not due to old pits,” Ray, the agency manager, wrote in a memo distributed months earlier within the oil division that urged agency leaders not to allow Citation to restart injection.

May, the agency’s consultant, echoed these rebuttals during the meeting and said the state’s evidence pointed to an injection problem. She concluded her presentation with a warning: Citation must change its injection practices in the Bayou.

“If y’all want to start injecting again,” she told company representatives, “I think we’re going to have to look at those pressures and the volumes very carefully.”

The meeting ended without a resolution.

“They Wore Us Out”

Over the next four months, Citation and state regulators would continue to debate the terms of restarting the Bayou. Neither side budged. By the time they gathered for another face-off in March 2024, oil division leaders appeared weary of fighting.

May and the Halff geologists from the consulting firm began by again insisting that Citation substantially reduce pressures in order to be allowed to restart a handful of wells. But even as they presented their case, Citation representatives including Lewis, the engineer, and Bob Redweik, a company vice president, repeatedly spoke over them. After more than two hours of disagreement, Redweik and Citation’s attorney ended the meeting abruptly. “We’re not going anywhere,” Redweik said.

Several top oil division officials attended, including Strickland, McGinnis and commission attorney Tyler Trout. They remained largely silent throughout.

The next week, Trout tried to end the impasse by passing along a memo from Citation.

“In an effort to reach an agreement and move this situation forward,” Trout wrote to top oil division officials and May, “would we consider meeting Citation in the middle as far as recommended injection pressures are concerned?”

May stood firm. “From Halff’s standpoint, our recommendations aren’t going to change,” she responded, adding that it would ultimately be up to agency leaders.

In early April, the agency went with a compromise, approving a plan to bring seven of Citation’s 19 Bayou injection wells back online. The company would be able to inject at pressures higher than Halff had recommended, though less than Citation had requested.

Current and former employees say that the decision to restart injection came from the top of the oil division, including Strickland and McGinnis, among others — bypassing staff who objected to the plan. Like Strickland, McGinnis did not respond to requests for comment.

“They wore us out,” said an agency manager who spoke on the condition of anonymity to protect their job.

Before injection restarted, three oil division officials chosen by Strickland conducted a walkthrough of the Bayou with Halff and Citation, according to an email from Strickland. The rest of the division was left in the dark. That same day, a pollution abatement manager noted in an email to the commission’s general counsel that agency critics of the plan had not been invited.

Around the time agency leaders allowed Citation to restart injection in the Bayou, staff were drafting an extensive contempt case against the company for rule violations in other parts of the state, according to public records obtained by The Frontier and ProPublica. Field staff and consultants were still turning up considerable problems related to Citation’s injection, including excessive pressures at the sites of destructive eruptions of wastewater. The staff complaint called for the agency to issue fines and to terminate well permits. But oil division leaders never signed the paperwork for the case.

There was ongoing trouble in the Bayou as well. Weeks after Citation restarted injection, field staff discovered a “severely contaminated” private water well nearby that had been polluted by oil field waste. Testing showed high levels of salt as well as the “highest levels of bromide that we have ever sampled,” according to internal emails, referring to another chemical constituent of oil and gas waste that poses a public health risk. (The landowners declined to comment because of an ongoing lawsuit against Citation, but according to court records, they do not drink from the well. The company, which has fought the family’s claims, says in a court filing that it has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars addressing the pollution on their land as part of a plan approved by the commission.)

By the end of 2024, oil division leaders had allowed six more Citation wells back online, bringing the total to 13. And the next spring, the agency closed the Bayou investigation, along with several others related to Citation, without taking further action.

Collection of New Complaints

In the year and a half since the Bayou case closed, several of the oil division staff who had pushed agency leaders to punish Citation have left the agency, as have a handful of senior leaders. Staffers told The Frontier and ProPublica they grew frustrated with the agency’s unwillingness to crack down on repeat corporate offenders that agency staff had spent months — at times, years — investigating.

Tracy Case, an attorney for the oil and gas division, admitted as much at a national conference for oil regulators in Oklahoma City in May. “I’ve been there 11 years doing this and we’ve never pursued what we call our ‘bad actors,’” she said, according to a recording of a meeting obtained by the news outlets. She explained that the oil division is extremely short-staffed while dealing with hundreds of potential enforcement cases at any one time. An agency spokesperson declined to comment on behalf of Case.

Less than a third of the roughly 750 enforcement cases filed by the oil division in the agency’s administrative law courts since 2023 have resulted in punishment so far, according to a review by The Frontier and ProPublica. The average fine given out by the agency was about $1,700. The most common punishment was a $500 fine, combined with using company insurance money to plug unused wells.

Neither the Oklahoma Corporation Commission nor Halff responded to questions about whether the consulting firm still has a role at the state agency.

At the Bayou, nearly all of Citation’s wastewater injection wells are back on, many operating at pressures beyond Halff’s recommendations. And industry data indicates that Citation has ramped up oil production to pre-shutdown levels even as evidence of new purges continues to emerge. In September, fresh layers of salt — residue of the wastewater — covered the dirt near yellowish puddles of standing water. Nearby, streaks of oil shone on the ground. The preceding weeks had been hot and dry, with hardly any rain.

In early October, an agency field staffer requested that Citation install a specialized well in the Bayou to pump out polluted groundwater, according to a report in the agency’s incident database.

A slew of new pollution complaints against Citation have continued to appear in that state database, including more than 60 spills and leaks at well sites over the past year. Among the complaints were three purges that blew out in southern Oklahoma over the last three months. All those investigations remain active, according to state records.

Another ongoing complaint against Citation originated about 10 miles east of the Bayou, where a rancher named Mike Faulkner noticed an unusual amount of salt water gurgling to the surface and flowing down a creek on his land in April. Nearby, dozens of Citation wells pump wastewater underground.

In response, Citation once again blamed the pollution on old drilling practices, according to an email from one of the company’s engineers to the Oklahoma Corporation Commission.

Nevertheless, the agency told the company to temporarily shut down some of its nearby injection wells, and, according to Faulkner, the purge on his land dried up for the first time in years.

“That tells me that they know the why and the how of that saltwater purging,” he said in July.

The agency also instructed Citation to install monitoring wells to test for pollution and to build a pit with a rock dam on Faulkner’s land to catch the polluted water, along with a fence to keep the cattle out.

But in the months since, the agency has given Citation multiple extensions on the deadline to build the dam and the fencing. In September, Faulkner learned that the agency granted Citation yet another extension — until December, seven months after his initial pollution report.

As of October, he said, the wells where the state had asked Citation to pause operations are injecting — at reduced pressure.

Faulkner said he is fed up with Citation’s yearslong pattern of degrading his pastures. But he blames state officials for their unwillingness to rein in the company.

“They’re like a spoiled kid,” he said. “They’ve just gotten away with it for a long time.”

stories.title: Cybersecurity CEO Indicted for Allegedly Scamming Millions From Ransomware Victims
stories.summary: The post Cybersecurity CEO Indicted for Allegedly Scamming Millions From Ransomware Victims appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A webpage with the words: “The World’s Leading Experts in IT, Cloud Management, & Counter Cyber Terrorism. Under Attack? Watch This Video Immediately!” A video appears showing a man with short cropped hair wearing a suit and tie with the caption: John Pistole, Former Deputy Director, FBI.
stories.body:
A federal grand jury indicted MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi last month for allegedly defrauding clients of his ransomware data recovery business, which was the subject of a 2019 ProPublica investigation.

A Florida man who was the subject of a 2019 investigation by ProPublica was indicted last month on federal charges that he defrauded clients of his ransomware data recovery firm.

According to the Justice Department, the man, Zohar Pinhasi, told customers he could recover their encrypted files without having to pay hackers, when, in reality, he paid the ransom and charged victims a hefty fee on top.

The indictment mirrors the findings from ProPublica’s 2019 article “ The Trade Secret ,” which centered on Pinhasi and his scheme. The outlet found that the ransomware victims were being harmed twice: once by the hackers, who locked their targets’ files and demanded ransom, and a second time by MonsterCloud, Pinhasi’s Florida-based data recovery firm, which misled its clients about not paying ransoms.

Read More

“By falsely claiming to decrypt ransomware without paying off the ransomers, the defendant re-victimized his clients while extracting a hefty profit for himself,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella said in an Oct. 7 press release. “Our Office will vigorously prosecute ransomware attackers who prey on Americans from across the world and those who cynically profit from their criminal activity.”

When ProPublica published its story in 2019, ransomware was growing into one of the world’s most pervasive cyberthreats. Hackers locked the data of governments, schools and businesses, holding the decryption key for a ransom payment, which they usually demanded in bitcoin and other types of difficult-to-trace cryptocurrency.

ProPublica’s reporting focused on how U.S. industries, from data recovery firms like MonsterCloud to insurance giants that cover ransom payments, all fueled the extortion economy . Ransomware remains a widespread threat today, and the threat to national security has grown as hackers linked to hostile foreign governments are believed to use ransomware as a cover for espionage. The prevalence of AI tools is also making it easier for attackers to spread ransomware.

Pinhasi, who went by the alias Zack Green, told ProPublica in 2019 that MonsterCloud never promised clients that their data will be recovered by any particular method. “How we do it, it’s our problem,” he told ProPublica. “You will get your data back. Sit back, relax and enjoy the ride.” He called MonsterCloud’s data recovery methods a “trade secret.”

Pinhasi hung up when reached on his cellphone this month. A message left with a representative at MonsterCloud’s office phone number and a message left with his attorney were not returned. A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Pinhasi pleaded not guilty to the federal charges.

In its 2019 investigation, ProPublica interviewed MonsterCloud’s clients and ransomware experts and found that in certain cases the firm must have paid ransoms on behalf of clients. MonsterCloud’s services were particularly popular with local law enforcement agencies, who are loath to engage with or pay criminal hackers. Several interviewed by ProPublica at the time said they chose MonsterCloud to help them recover from ransomware because they believed the firm would never pay a ransom.

Pinhasi, who described himself to ProPublica as a former IT security intelligence officer for the Israeli military, said in 2019 that MonsterCloud handled up to 30 calls a day and had about 20 employees in South Florida as well as extensive global contacts.

Federal investigators found that, over the course of the scheme, Pinhasi allegedly charged clients more than $19 million and paid more than $8 million in ransom payments. In one example, Pinhasi made a ransom payment of about $8,200 but charged the client about $150,000. If convicted, he faces up to 20 years in prison.

In the Justice Department’s October press release, an FBI official said Pinhasi had “turned the victim’s crisis into his own profit center. This deception is unacceptable, and the FBI is committed to ensuring accountability for those who choose to victimize the very people who trusted them for help.”

The Justice Department did not address ProPublica’s 2019 finding that one of the FBI’s own was among Pinhasi’s associates at MonsterCloud. John Pistole, a former deputy director of the FBI under Robert Mueller, was prominently featured in a promotional video on MonsterCloud’s homepage. “Police departments, government agencies, hospitals, small business and Fortune 500 firms trust MonsterCloud to help recover from attacks and protect against new ones,” Pistole said in the video. “MonsterCloud’s proprietary technology and expertise protects their professional reputations and organizational integrity.”

Pistole was not mentioned by name in the Pinhasi indictment.

In 2019, Pinhasi touted MonsterCloud’s ties to law enforcement as evidence of its integrity. Pistole, who also headed the Transportation Security Administration under President Barack Obama, was listed on MonsterCloud’s website as the only member of its “Cyber Security Advisory Council.”

Pistole did not respond to a request for comment for this story. In a 2019 interview, he said he became acquainted with Pinhasi after MonsterCloud reached him through a speaker’s bureau and that MonsterCloud paid him indirectly through that group. He said Pinhasi scripted his testimonial and that he was well aware that in most cases — including MonsterCloud’s — the only way to decrypt data locked by ransomware is to pay the hackers. “That’s the business model as I understood it,” Pistole told ProPublica at the time. “Based on my experience and knowledge, ransom is paid and they facilitate the best practices moving forward.”

A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment on Pistole’s connection to MonsterCloud.

stories.title: Free the Kremlin’s Political Prisoners—and Stop Sending It New Ones
stories.summary: The Trump administration’s one-off deals won’t empty Russia’s prisons—especially while U.S. deportations are refilling them. The post Free the Kremlin’s Political Prisoners—and Stop Sending It New Ones appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

In late September, The Atlantic reported that U.S. President Donald Trump had greenlit plans to offer Russia sanctions relief in exchange for the release of political prisoners.

With peace talks still deadlocked after more than a year of U.S. diplomacy, sanctions remain a vital check on Russia’s ability to wage war against Ukraine. In the following weeks, however, Trump struck a diesel deal with Vladimir Putin and waived new sanctions on Russian oil and gas. This provoked backlash from Kyiv, but Trump insisted that he was making “great progress” with Russia, including on “hostage negotiations.”

Then, on October 21, the Kremlin freed Stephen Hubbard , a 74-year-old American citizen held in Russian captivity for over four years. In statements about the release , Trump said that the United States “was not required to give anything in return,” while admitting that enforcing tougher sanctions would have halted negotiations for Hubbard’s freedom.

As critics note, the release of Hubbard cost Putin little, and making concessions risks incentivizing the regime to take more hostages. At the same time, a glaring contradiction is being overlooked. While Washington negotiates to free some prisoners, its immigration policy is funneling new ones into Russia’s jails.

Who the Kremlin Holds

No one knows exactly how many people Russia has arbitrarily detained in connection with its war against Ukraine. The international human rights campaign People First! estimates tens of thousands; most are Ukrainian civilians imprisoned across Russia and occupied Ukraine. These “ghost prisoners” are held without formal charges. They are tortured and kept incommunicado, with no access to lawyers, relatives, or international organizations.

In occupied Crimea, where Russia has enforced one of its harshest regimes since 2014, Ukrainian authorities have identified 223 political prisoners, including 155 Crimean Tatars and many with serious health problems .

According to OVD-Info data , at least 2,368 people are currently imprisoned in Russia for political reasons. The number of politically motivated criminal proceedings is even higher, with more than 5,000 active cases.

The #free120 campaign puts the total number of critically ill political prisoners at 406. Every year, several die behind bars.

People First! calls for any negotiated peace agreement to prioritize the immediate release of all these captives, alongside the return of Ukrainian children forcibly taken to Russia, the repatriation of POWs held by both sides, and the release of Belarusians imprisoned for their anti-war views.

When it comes to hostage negotiations, which are often treated as a separate diplomatic track, priority should go to the most vulnerable: minors and the elderly, the seriously ill, torture victims, and those targeted for their sexuality, ethnicity, or faith. One-off exchanges offer no transparent or permanent mechanism for deciding who goes free.

In talks with Russia, Washington has long focused on freeing specific individuals, particularly its own citizens. In December 2022, for example, the Biden administration agreed to a controversial one-for-one exchange, trading notorious Russian arms dealer Victor Bout for Brittney Griner, an American basketball star imprisoned in Russia on drug charges.

Two years later, the United States orchestrated the biggest prisoner swap between Russia and Western countries since the Cold War. The Kremlin ultimately handed over 16 people—most of them Russian political prisoners—in exchange for eight FSB agents, hackers, and spies.

These releases were humanitarian achievements: unjustly imprisoned people regained their freedom, and lives were likely saved—even if the Russians among them were forced into exile . However, releases alone do not change what puts people behind bars. So long as the laws used to punish dissent remain in force, new cases will keep coming.

The John Coale Approach—and an Alternative

The Kremlin has denied holding any political prisoners or engaging in talks on sanctions relief with American officials. But Trump’s nomination of John Coale as U.S. envoy for hostage affairs suggests plans to replicate his strategy as special envoy to Belarus.

Having built a rapport with authoritarian leader Aleksander Lukashenko, Coale has secured the release of more than 500 political prisoners in exchange for easing U.S. sanctions. However, this has turned repression into a revolving door, with Minsk freeing certain people while continuing to imprison others on political grounds.

During Coale’s last meeting with Lukashenko in September, the United States hoped to free 200 more political prisoners. He came away with 25 people in return for lifting U.S. sanctions on two Belarusian companies. According to Viasna, a leading Belarusian human rights group, at least 10 others were prepared for release and then sent back to their cells, likely due to the outcome of the talks.

At least 88 5 political prisoners remain behind bars in Belarus today. Every one is a person with loved ones awaiting their release; under current U.S. policy, each is also a potential bargaining chip.

If the Senate confirms Coale’s new position, his portfolio will expand to include Russia, among other authoritarian countries. Negotiations with such regimes demand a consistent strategy to save lives and effect systemic change.

To this end, Washington should push for the following simultaneously:

the immediate release of Ukrainian civilians and political prisoners held by Russia;

the repeal of repressive legislation targeting freedom of speech and civil society organizations (such as the laws on military censorship, “foreign agents,” and “undesirable” organizations);

an end to the arbitrary use of anti-terrorism, anti-extremism, and national-security laws, including those on treason and espionage frequently used to target and severely punish political opponents and Ukrainian citizens.

At the very least, the United States should demand that the Kremlin disclose the identities and whereabouts of all detainees, and provide international organizations full access to them.

Handing the Kremlin New Hostages

Unfortunately, Washington is helping refill the Kremlin’s “hostage bank.” Under the Trump administration’s deportation policy, Russians facing political persecution are being denied asylum in the United States and returned to their home country.

According to the BBC , removals surpassed 1,200 in 2025, up from 222 in 2023. Among these deportees were anti-war dissidents and army deserters, some of whom were handed military summonses, sent to the front, or arrested upon their return to Russia.

The imprisonment of activist Leonid Melekhin is a case in point. Melekhin spent 10 months in U.S. immigration detention, only to have his asylum bid rejected in July 2025. He was then deported to Russia, where he was arrested upon arrival on “terrorism” charges. On October 5, a Russian court sentenced Melekhin to six years in prison.

The activist’s time in U.S. detention reportedly “broke him” (Melekhin’s state-appointed lawyer in Russia claims that he “asked to be sent back” to Russia). The conditions in ICE detention facilities are indeed concerning. As of this writing, Russian asylum seekers in at least three detention centers have joined hunger strikes to protest alleged mistreatment and poor conditions.

The Trump administration can act preemptively to support those facing political persecution in their home country. It should halt deportations, guarantee fair asylum hearings, end prolonged detentions, and protect dissidents, journalists, and those who refuse to fight.

Freeing political prisoners is among diplomacy’s most humane goals. To have the greatest impact, Washington should pair negotiations for releases with sustained pressure to dismantle the laws that fill prisons—and ensure that those who escape persecution find refuge, not a return ticket to a cell.

stories.title: President Apocalypse
stories.summary: While Trump campaigns for a Nobel Peace Prize, his war on humanity’s only home continues unabated. The post President Apocalypse appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

Originally published in TomDispatch .

Do I even faintly believe the times I’m living in? The simple answer is: no.

Every now and then, I try to imagine going back in time to tell my long-dead parents about the world of President Donald Trump, which just happens to still be mine as well. Of course, they simply wouldn’t have believed it, not for a single second.

To put it in the context of their time on this planet, the only equivalent I can imagine would be if Sen. Joseph McCarthy, that anticommunist nightmare-and-a-half of the 1950s, hadn’t flamed out, been censured by the Senate, and died young but somehow had made it to the White House. But even he undoubtedly would have fallen short in terms of chaos and cruelty, if judged by the standards of Trump World. A President McCarthy might have been catastrophic for America, but Trump is on another level, an apocalyptic one.

Trump’s capacity for ushering in world-wrecking havoc is made possible by a character constructed almost entirely of flaws. His second term has been defined by global aggression and hostility. Yet he recently complained bitterly — and in a fashion it’s hard to imagine any other politician ever doing — because he wasn’t awarded a Nobel Peace Prize. As he put it , “The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel peace prize, but didn’t. And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway, and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision.”

This is not only a petty man, but also a delusional one. As president, Trump has presided over more than 20 military interventions, armed conflicts, and outright wars who nonetheless swears that he “settled” eight conflicts and should have “ won 8 Nobel Peace Prizes, not just 1 .” This includes a war between Egypt and Ethiopia that, of course, never happened and a failing war with Iran that drags on to this day.

If you’re going to “end” a war with bombs and missiles, then there are, of course, going to be casualties. A few thousand or more Iranians killed , obviously, and tens of thousands injured, not to mention ever-rising American casualties.

Frighteningly, the Iran war may not even be enough for him. He’s already starting to hint (if there even is such a thing as “hinting” in the all-too-blunt world of Donald Trump) that he might join Saudi Arabia in taking on the Houthi rebels in Yemen. “We’re going to look at it” was how he put it . I should really have added “again” there, since he essentially began his second term in office by attacking those same Houthis — killing large numbers of civilians in the process. But after the U.S. burned through $1 billion and failed to even achieve air superiority in Yemen, Trump ended the stalemate. Despite having vowed the Houthis would be “completely annihilated,” he announced a cessation of hostilities last May, leaving the group in control of most of Yemen’s populated areas.

Given American history — think the wars in Korea, Vietnam , Cambodia, Afghanistan, and Iraq, among other places — there’s nothing faintly strange about endless American military operations thousands and thousands of miles away from Washington, D.C., even for a president who said, upon taking office in 2025, that he would measure success by “the wars we never get into.”

A Grim Presidency

You would hardly know it from the mainstream press but one of those 20 Trumpian conflicts is the forever war in Somalia . And that war has an increasing domestic component. Recently, the Department of Homeland Security raided the home of Somali American Rep. Ilhan Omar in the Washington, D.C., area, aiming in some fashion or other to discover information that might help denaturalize her and so make it possible to eject her from this country.

As the president put it on Truth Social, Omar “left Somalia with NOTHING, and is now reportedly worth more than 44 Million Dollars.” Of course, who would know better about such things than the president of the United States who, in these years, is estimated to have made literally billions of dollars while in office ?

And yet, the never-ending war in Somalia, the nearby conflict we may reenter against the Houthis, and the failed war in Iran should be considered the lesser of the potential disasters that will sooner or later be associated with Trump. After all, he clearly has the urge to do nothing less than end this very world of ours , at least as we’ve known it, even if in a distinctly slow-motion fashion.

I’m not even thinking about nuclear weapons (although he admittedly still is ). No, I’m thinking about the president who, at the United Nations in 2025, called climate change “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world.” And since then, he has indeed done everything he could think of to ensure that this planet would get hotter yet. His Environmental Protection Agency, for instance, has recently repealed “rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas.” And that’s just to start down a long list of what should truly be considered Donald Trump’s ultimate war on this planet of ours — including blocking wind power development and doing the same with solar power.

All of this is happening as global warming reaches unprecedented levels, sea level rise is accelerating, northern forests and tundra are releasing more carbon dioxide than they absorb, the Greenland ice sheet has lost about 129 gigatons of ice (or roughly 129 billion metric tons), and other major ecological systems like tropical coral reefs , the Amazon rainforest , and Antarctica’s ice sheet are being pushed toward catastrophic tipping points.

While Trump campaigns for eight Nobel Peace Prizes, his war on humanity’s only home continues unabated, a slow-motion destruction that threatens us all. My parents couldn’t have imagined a leader in the White House who would put McCarthy to shame and push the country — and the world — to the precipice of doom: a commander-in-chief worthy of the name President Apocalypse.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

stories.title: Turbulent Times Call For Experimental Law
stories.summary: The post Turbulent Times Call For Experimental Law appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Experiments with the rule of law around the world are creating the kind of resiliency we need in our era of uncertainty.

MUNICH — Shortly after wandering into the Munich Urban Colab this summer, I found myself trying to follow an intense conversation in German about the city’s new experiment with autonomous buses. A local official, clocking my curious puzzlement, offered an aside in English: “We are asking ourselves: ‘What does it mean when the law is an experiment too?’”

No question may be more essential to governance in our era of dangerous uncertainty.

Global warming is accelerating faster than global treaties on mitigation can be negotiated. Climate catastrophes occur with a sudden ferocity beyond what current adaptation laws anticipate. Biological threats surface and kill before public health responses can be formulated. And AI is evolving faster and more wildly than regulators or lawmakers, or even its designers, expect.

All this dizzying unpredictability is undermining traditional legal structures. The threat is not just to the rule of law, but to the very nature of law, at least as humans have conceived it.

Our societies have long considered the law a slow and steady force, “the essential foundation of stability and order” in the words of J. William Fulbright. To that end, law is backward-looking — “the government of the living by the dead,” according to Oliver Wendell Holmes. The lawmaking process in republics and democracies is age-old: observe a problem, study its particularities, debate solutions and then carve out a rule that will endure for years or decades.

But what happens when the future arrives faster than your regional regulator or local parliament can make a rule?

The emerging answer is experimental law or, in Germany, where Munich is a hotbed, Experimentierklauseln . “Experimental clauses” refer to sections and parts of laws that are made flexible, often for set time periods, to allow for real-time adaptation or alteration in response to changing threats, climate or technology.

The shift toward such experimentation has begun, albeit slowly, in only certain areas of the law. Contract law and administrative law, especially where they touch on technology or other advanced sectors of the economy, are becoming more fluid.

Contracts, once used to protect against all contingencies, are now written more openly — explicitly anticipating new knowledge and adjustments. Among startups and innovation-oriented companies, written agreements are less likely to specify payments for specific work at specific times and more likely to establish processes for collaboration and shared decision-making.

For example, start-ups use Agile contracts with vendors that, instead of pledging a final digital product at a price, set parameters of a creative process involving a test phase, iterative feedback loops and product benchmarks. Biotech startups rely on a “relational contract” with manufacturers to create a collaboration framework that includes regular meetings, shared lab notes and a commitment to use best efforts to scale a prototype.

Meanwhile, smart contracts have become commonplace in supply chains to allow for real-time changes in inventory levels. Union contracts in digital workplaces often incorporate adaptive provisions — “continuous bargaining” in 21st-century labor parlance — with guidelines for how workers participate across the lifecycles of systems and products.

Modern tech procurement uses what’s called “Dynamic Service Level Agreements” that feature automatic updates, scalable license adjustments, and continuous remote monitoring and interventions by seller and buyer. “Data Processing Agreements” within cloud contracts dynamically adjust data handling and security protocols as privacy regulations and digital risks shift. In some cases, AI agents have written contracts in code rather than in English. Put simply, some contracts now write themselves.

Similarly, regulatory agencies and public administrations have moved away from the time-consuming traditional rulemaking process, since rules quickly become outdated in a world so strange and fast-changing. Instead, agencies and administrative judges, particularly in advanced economies, are more likely to offer “guidance” — advisories, memos, letters or protocols that are regularly tweaked or edited in response to updated knowledge and changing circumstances.

These shifts point toward an emerging and quite radical recognition, especially in law, that extreme uncertainty is not a problem to be solved, but a reality and even an ally. The fact that the future is too hard for anyone to know is leveling. The regulator, the regulated and the everyday person all know the same thing: almost nothing.

The act of lawmaking then becomes a great collaboration between governments and experts and firms and workers and the regular people most affected. And that collaboration is a search, never-ending, for improvements and innovations and solutions.

Such collaboration turns lawmaking as we know it on its head. Implementation is required first to understand what the policy should be. In this new paradigm, resilience is grounded in fragility. Resilience does not come from buffering organizations against known risks, but by designing them to show quickly when they are broken, so they can be reconfigured. It is a kind of deliberately induced and carefully controlled institutional fragility. Strain is immediately apparent, triggering investigation and countermeasures well before it ramifies into catastrophe.

“Experimental clauses allow for real-time adaptation in response to changing threats, climate or technology.”

Climate Changes The Law

The stakes of achieving this new, more open mentality are expressed perhaps most clearly in our response to global warming. In the 2022 book, “Fixing the Climate: Strategies for an Uncertain World,” Columbia Law School’s Charles F. Sabel and UC San Diego’s David G. Victor argue that decades of top-down global climate diplomacy — from the Kyoto Protocol to the Paris Agreement — have failed because they rely on inflexible global treaties.

Treaties are among the oldest forms of law. But climate treaties are outdated the moment they are signed, because the climate is changing too quickly. And they don’t reflect the reality that climate change impacts — and opportunities to mitigate and adapt to climate change — are very different depending on location and context. (Sea level rise is not an issue in Mongolia; glacial melting does not plague Phoenix). The only viable way to make law and government is thus through relentless, highly structured and broadly collaborative local experimentation. This model, they noted, is neither “top down” nor “bottom up” but both at the same time.

“Our central aim is to reorient our current climate change regime away from failed efforts based on ex ante global consensus, and toward a system anchored in local and sectoral experimentalism and learning,” they wrote .

This local experimentalist mindset is emerging especially in the metro regions of countries that have advanced economies and histories of collaborative lawmaking and regulation.

Two places that best fit that description are Singapore, which was built on deep cooperation between government technocrats and industry, and Germany’s bigger cities.

Experimental law first emerged in West Germany during the 1950s as a pragmatic mechanism for the Länder, or states, to exploit their autonomy under the 1949 Basic Law. Faced with ideological divisions and a lack of national precedent for building a post-authoritarian society, municipal and state agencies used “trial clauses” to break legacy rules on welfare, housing and local administrative reorganizations without setting precedents or locking local governments into long-term mandates. The first official Experimentierklauseln allowed public schools to violate rigid curricular and education standards and test pedagogies, grading systems and models of comprehensive schools.

Experimental clauses fell out of fashion in the late 20th century but were revived for new challenges in the 21st century. In 2008, the Upper Saxony town of Bohmte, Germany , used an experimental clause to do something otherwise illegal: eradicate traffic lanes, street lines, traffic lights and stop signs to combat chronic speeding, utilizing a Dutch idea called shared space .

Over the last decade, climate change and advances in technology and transportation inspired so much local experimentalism that the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action issued an official “Guide for Formulating Experimentation Clauses” in 2024. The guide runs 34 pages but contains three main rules: All experimental clauses must have an expiration date, a clear geographical or sectoral boundary, and rigorous evaluation.

Ask the federal ministry staff for a signature example, and you’ll hear about a Hamburg hospital that couldn’t get cancer tissue samples to a laboratory in time because of city traffic. The hospital wanted to use a drone instead, but German aviation regulations strictly forbid drones from flying “beyond the visual line of sight” of their operators over settled urban areas.

Instead of waiting years for federal airspace reform, Hamburg relied on experimental clauses to deviate from the federal Air Traffic Act for 18 months. During that time, the city-state established the U-Space Sandbox, a 30-square-kilometer experimental airspace over the Port of Hamburg.

Officials of the local and national governments worked with two German companies, Droniq and DFS Deutsche Flugsicheruntegration, to test the integration of drones with manned aviation. The experimentation eventually produced guidance and rules for a drone air traffic system, which are being incorporated into drafts of Germany’s federal U-Space Act.

“Climate treaties are outdated the moment they are signed, because the climate is changing too quickly.”

Living With Experimental Law

In Munich, I spent an evening inside one product of experimental law: an unusual new house at Goerzerstrasse 128, in the southeast neighborhood of Giesing. Munich, like so many cities, suffers from high housing prices and rents. The city held a competition for alternative solutions, and a self-organized housing syndicate won. It then used experimental clauses to deviate from strict German building codes.

The building was constructed with simple wood and cheap corrugated iron — what residents call “Favela-style” — and operates internally as a massive “shed flat.” The design is energy-efficient, and the roof captures rainwater in an underground cistern and feeds it directly back into the local groundwater table to combat drought. Read Noema in print.

The cost exceeded 3 million euros, drawn from public subsidies and private loans. But that’s cheap, given its scale. For now, 14 people — 13 adults and a six-year-old — share the open architecture, with frequent visitors. (A rock band was just leaving as I arrived.) The building is designed so it could be divided into at least nine separate apartments. While one-bedroom apartments in Munich rent for 1,700 euros a month, rent at Gorzer 128 is about 460 euros per person.

Gorzer 128 and other experiments helped inspire a national experimental clause called “Construction Turbo” (Section 246e of the German Federal Building Code), which allows municipalities to bypass existing planning standards until the end of 2030. The only unhappiness has come from neighbors who don’t like the building’s appearance (a jumble of metal and wood, quite different than the single-family craftsman homes on the street) and have been slow to engage with residents. Experimental law offers no cure for NIMBYism, at least not yet.

Beyond Gorzer 128, Munich’s experimental laws are most associated with efforts to transform streetscapes. A signal success is on the Kolumbusstraße, which a few years ago was a standard urban artery, lined with 120 concrete parking slots and choked with traffic.

Oliver May-Beckmann, who leads the MCube mobility cluster at the Technical University of Munich (TUM), says his group used an experimental clause to close the street to traffic for six months to create a Sommerstraße (Summer Street). Some drivers and residents complained to local officials. But because the project was a temporary and science-driven Reallabor , or real-world laboratory, politicians could push responsibility onto May-Beckmann and the scientists. “They’d say, ‘It’s just an experiment, let’s wait for the data,” he recalls.

For half a year , Kolumbusstraße became a green space where children could play, residents could spend time and new forms of mobility were tested. The transformation was deliberately temporary, and after six months, the street returned to its previous state. But the evaluation produced a striking result: 66% of residents supported making the changes permanent. Whether and how to turn the experiment into a lasting transformation is now a decision for the City of Munich.

MCube also used an experimental clause to test a car-sharing strategy in Nymphenburg, an affluent neighborhood that houses Munich’s botanical garden. For 20 years, Germany’s car industry — BMW, Mercedes, Sixt — had been testing different forms of free-floating vehicle-sharing to try to cut emissions, but it just put more cars on the street because people used shared vehicles on top of their own. In MCube’s test, 10 local families gave up their private cars for 18 months, and MCube bought five electric cars, plugged into charging stations in an underground garage, for the families to share. It was a closed group — the sharing was just between the 10 households, and you knew who had the car before you.

The families communicated with each other and shared the cars well. MCube also discovered that when people know a car is always nearby, they were willing to pay significantly more in regular payments for access than they would pay with one-off models. MCube is now working with both BMW and Sixt, the Bavaria-based rental car company, to spread the model around Germany. The experimental clause is still in effect and is being used to test alternative car-sharing models in three other Munich neighborhoods.

Experimental clauses offer flexibility but demand deep collaboration with business, governments and everyday people, May-Beckmann says. Take MINGA , a new project that plans to put autonomous buses on Munich’s streets this fall. (Minga is both the name for Munich in the Bavarian dialect and an acronym for Münchens Automatisierter Integrations-Nahverkehr mit Gesellschaftlicher Akzeptanz, or “Munich Automated Public Transport with Ridepooling, Solo Bus and Bus Platoons.”

The project, which uses driverless vehicles without a set schedule or route, is enabled by experimental clauses derived from 2021 amendments to Section 1i of the German Road Traffic Act. The German government is providing 13 million euros in funds. MAN, a German commercial vehicle manufacturer, built the buses. Technical University of Munich scientists have worked on the software, the public transport administration is preparing to run the buses, and the city of Munich plans to operate the service for two years under experimental clauses and then evaluate it. Finally, it requires people to sign up, primarily to bridge the “first-mile/last-mile” gap of getting people to public transit hubs.

Experimental clauses, at their best, create space and permission for systems integration. That’s nearly impossible in conventional governance, where decisions are made sequentially, and services and programs are added one by one.

“Our goal is transferring knowledge into prototypes and bringing those into real life,” says May-Beckmann. “It’s crucial in Europe that mobility innovation isn’t just about a new car; it’s about a system. How do you integrate autonomous driving, city development, climate change and energy? We get funding to have industry and public administration work for us as a system.”

“All experimental clauses must have an expiration date, a clear geographical or sectoral boundary, and rigorous evaluation.”

Experiments In Sunshine & Medicine

The desire to experiment with law is not exclusively German. Barcelona placed the 22@ Innovation District under experimental law to test drones. In the UK, Bethesda and other Welsh cities have employed experimental clauses for “ Sunshine Tariffs ” to encourage renewable energy use. South Korea carved out an experimental exception in its transportation laws to install a hydrogen-powered mobility system in Gyeongsangbuk-do. In Japan, the experimental mantle is carried by the “Future Design” movement, where citizens in towns like Yahaba wear differently colored robes to design infrastructure plans for future generations.

If democracy doesn’t have to be part of the legal equation, then East Asia might be the world’s leader. Singapore, the world leader in temporary regulations, has built a financial powerhouse by permitting banking and fintech experiments for decades. More recently, it has been applying experimentalism to medicine. An ongoing Health Sciences Authority experiment allows low- to medium-risk AI medical software to be used in public hospitals before formal registration. If the AI performs well for 12 months under clinician oversight, it can get an accelerated pathway to permanent approval.

More broadly, China and India have survived and prospered during rapid transitions by making experimentation a foundational principle of governance, often at the municipal or provincial levels.

In his 2024 book “Experimentalist Constitutions,” Peking University legal scholar Yueduan Wang details the Chinese government’s use of “experimental zones” to deviate from national law. In several areas, including green energy and mobility, municipalities have explicit legislative permission to try things. For example, the Shenzhen People’s Congress passed the 2025-2026 “Decision on Amending the Regulations of Shenzhen Special Economic Zone on Intelligent Connected Vehicles,” which allows fully driverless commercial taxis to bypass national safety standards.

India has embedded what it calls “regulatory sandbox” clauses directly into legislative updates. The Telecommunication Act of 2023 explicitly created a live testing environment that exempts companies from standard licensing fees to test 6G internet. Gujarat, where Narendra Modi served as chief before becoming national prime minister, is an epicenter of experimentation. It houses India’s first operational “smart city,” Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City), between Ahmedabad and Gandhinagar, to test flexible financial regulations. Many of its startups use an “interoperable sandbox” to temporarily bypass rules on corporate governance, liquidity, capital minimums, reporting timelines and marketing as they test hybrid fintech products.

Experimental Enough For AI?

Despite successes in fintech, mobility and housing, it is unclear whether experimental law will be fast or flexible enough for the ethereal, borderless realm of artificial intelligence.

In Germany, companies working with AI complain that experimental law remained too slow and earthbound to keep up. Ironically, they blame the European Union’s attempts to “lead” on experimental law and AI for the failure.

In 2024, the EU embraced experimental law with its landmark AI Act. Article 57 of the AI Act included an explicit mandate for experimental law — every member state was required to establish at least one national “AI regulatory sandbox” by August 2026. But the mandate made the program politically divisive within several countries. In a dozen member states, including Germany and France, governments couldn’t even agree on which national agency or authority would establish their sandbox. The EU acknowledged the dysfunction this summer, pushing the deadline for a national AI mandate back a year to August 2027, via the AI Omnibus .

Few in Europe’s AI policymaking community expect to meet that deadline. The trouble goes beyond the EU’s slow bureaucracy. It’s hard to employ experimental law when you’re terrified of real impacts and results. Notably, the AI Act doesn’t require experimental deployment of AI regulation in the real world. As a result, those nations that are moving toward an AI regulatory sandbox are limiting experiments to theoretical exercises or purely legal assessments. But it’s impossible to create experimental laws for AI in the real world if you won’t experiment with AI in the real world.

In Munich, Till Klein, head of regulation at the non-profit “appliedAI Institute for Europe,” says that regulatory sandboxes that do exist for AI simply have too many restrictions to be useful. “Policymakers act like sandboxes will fix all the new rules,” says Klein. “But a sandbox is more like a sniper rifle than a shotgun; your experiment has to be precise for it to be meaningful.”

His colleague Demian Niemeyer, a lawyer and senior AI regulatory expert at appliedAI, sees the choke point as cultural. “People trained in law here are trained in a ‘Bismarck mindset,’” he says. “They are incredibly risk-averse. If you want to make something better and understand risks, you need a trial-and-error mindset.”

The paradox is that fear of applying experimental law to AI has left AI running free, well beyond law and regulation. Another fear also hamstrings experimental law: fear of regulatory capture.

That’s understandable, since effective experimental law requires regulators to collaborate closely with companies and stakeholders. Experimental law challenges the conception of regulation and law as walls between the watcher and the watched.

“The paradox is that fear of applying experimental law to AI has left AI running free, well beyond law and regulation.”

In 2024 and 2025, fear of capture stirred controversy and delayed the drafting of Germany’s federal Reallabore-Gesetz (Regulatory Sandboxes) Act, an attempt to go beyond experimental clauses on particular subjects and create a broader framework for experimental law.

The Social Democrats, left-wing groups and some scholars argue that broad authorization of experimental clauses risks turning into backdoor-lobbying channels for Big Tech and powerful corporations seeking exemptions from labor, safety and privacy laws. Most of the objections were AI-focused.

In response, the proposed law’s backers incorporated regulatorisches Lernen (regulatory learning) as a sandbox objective. When a project is approved under an experimental clause, the outcomes cannot remain hidden. The law requires continuous evaluation of the testing, and the resulting insights must be reported transparently. There are limited exclusions for genuine intellectual property.

The law also seeks to avoid narrow regulatory discussions between a company and a government agency via a “Regulatory Sandboxes Innovation Portal.” The portal is supposed to facilitate broad co-creation of law by connecting stakeholders from business, academia, public administration and civil society.

The legislation, renamed the Bundeserprobungsgesetz (Federal Proving Act), passed the Bundestag in late June. A second legislative body, the Bundesrat, would formally enact it as law in September. At the Munich Urban Colab, the immediate reaction was uncertainty. People would have to experiment with the new law and see.

stories.title: Long After Maui Fire, Residents Found With High Levels of Toxic Metals in Their Bodies
stories.summary: More than a year after a devastating wildfire destroyed the Hawaiian town of Lahaina, residents were found to have high levels of arsenic and other toxic metals in their bodies. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
This article was originally published by Grist , in partnership with The Intercept , and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

Damage from the 2023 fire that destroyed the Hawaiian town of Lahaina. Matt McClain / The Washington Post via Getty Images via Grist

More than a year after a devastating wildfire destroyed the Hawaiian town of Lahaina, residents were found to have high levels of arsenic and other toxic metals in their bodies.

In August of 2023, a series of wildfires broke out across Maui, killing more than 100 people, destroying thousands of homes, and causing billions of dollars in damage. Noelani Ahia, who is Indigenous Kanaka Maoli and cofounder of Maui Medic Healers Hui, helped mobilize nearly 600 volunteers in Lahaina, including doctors, nurses, and therapists.

Three years later, the housing and health crises remain acute. Maui Medic Healers Hui runs a free clinic, but Ahia wishes it had 10 more to address the community’s needs. “The fire may be out, but the catastrophe is not over by any stretch of the imagination,” she said.

The devastation extended well beyond the lives lost and buildings destroyed. Research published last year by researchers with the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, found that more than 1 in 5 residents had reduced lung function.

Now, new research from the same project has found elevated levels of toxic metals in the island’s residents months after the fires, with higher exposure associated with impaired lung function. The findings offer further evidence that the health consequences of catastrophic wildfires can persist long after the flames are extinguished and the smoke clears.

“What we consider and sometimes look at as a one-time event isn’t really one-time anymore,” Alika Maunakea, who is Kanaka Maoli and codirector of MauiWES, told Grist .

Researchers don’t yet know how much of the contamination came from the fires and how much was already present in the environment. That distinction matters as wildfires increasingly race through towns like Lahaina and cities like Los Angeles, where burning of homes, cars, and infrastructure can leave contaminants that people encounter for months or years afterward.

“We have traditionally thought about wildfire exposure primarily through the lens of smoke,” Maunakea said in a press release. “But when an entire community burns, we are dealing with a much more complicated exposure environment.” Researchers must also understand what contaminants were already present, what the fire may have released, and what entered residents’ bodies, he said.

The research, which studied 1,400 adults across Maui six to 18 months after the fires, measured 24 metals in urine samples. It found that participants had higher concentrations of several metals than people in a nationwide health survey conducted before the fires. That included 2.2 times as much arsenic, 2.3 times as much barium, and 3.8 times as much manganese. Antimony, which is used in flame retardant materials and has been previously linked to lung irritation, stomach pain, and other symptoms, was found at levels nearly 40 times higher.

Because the researchers lack comparable data from before the fires, they could not determine how much of the metal exposure resulted from the disaster. Maunakea told Grist that answering that question is the next step for the project, which has received a $3.6 million grant from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences. That work will include investigating whether and to what degree past agricultural and industrial activity contributed to the contamination.

“It’s important to realize that these are all part of settler colonialism,” Ahia said. “So what we’re looking at is confounding factors that are to the detriment of the health of our local people.”

Decades of plantation agriculture altered water systems, introduced herbicides, and displaced native plants, leaving a legacy on the islands that is still felt today. Disasters like fires and storms can compound those ongoing environmental problems.

“If we begin the story when the fire starts, we miss the decisions that shaped the landscape and the community’s ability to respond,” said Katie Kamelamela, who is Indigenous Kanaka Maoli and an assistant professor at Arizona State University based in Hawaii. “Micro climate change acts on places already shaped by histories of land ownership, water diversion, development, and unequal access to resources.”

Kamelamela said true recovery must look beyond the fire. “I want recovery to be measured by whether people can remain in their communities, care for ʻāina, and pass on their knowledge and practices in place,” she said, using the Hawaiian word for land, which carries deeper meaning and relationship than property or mere place. “Rebuilding should not recreate the same conditions that left people at risk. Caring for ʻāina and caring for people need to be funded and planned together.”

Maunakea said the multitude of intersecting pressures is one reason why he wanted to pursue this research. As climate change continues to accelerate, longstanding issues facing Native Hawaiians like housing, the harms of tourism, and the legacy of plantations can amplify problems. “We worry that disasters like this that we experience on Maui, as well as the floods and other storms that we’re experiencing now, is just going to continue widening the gaps in health disparities that already exist in those populations,” he said.

Moving forward, the project will not just identify health risks but also help residents respond to them. Study participants receive their results, discuss them, and meet with health professionals. “People now know that there’s these types of potential hazards, and what to do about them is a big concern,” Maunakea said. “We still don’t have all the answers for sure, but we are taking the next steps to get a better picture and inform our community around it.”

— Joseph Lee , Grist
